items.title: Today's lesson
items.content:
A white-hot rail weld and a rust-free iron pillar open the lesson.

**Electron-dot diagrams** show metals giving electrons to non-metals, and a bulb test explains the **properties of ionic compounds**.

The reactivity series decides how each metal is **extracted**, through to the **thermit reaction** and **refining copper**; we end with **corrosion, galvanising and alloys**.

items.title: You already know
items.content:
• electronic configuration, valence electrons and the octet

• the reactivity series; oxidation and reduction

• iron rusts in moist air

items.title: By the end, you can
items.content:
**1.** Show how ionic compounds form, with electron-dot diagrams.

**2.** State and explain the properties of ionic compounds.

**3.** Outline how metals are extracted, by reactivity.

**4.** Describe electrolytic refining of copper.

**5.** Explain corrosion and its prevention.

• Left: at night, workers pour white-hot liquid iron into a gap between two railway tracks.

• Right: a family looks at an ancient iron pillar that has not rusted; the iron gate beside it is rusty.

**Answer to Question 1**

**Answer to Question 2**

items.text:
**What this shows**

Electron-dot structures for the formation of (a) sodium chloride and (b) magnesium chloride. Crosses are the metal's electrons; dots are the non-metal's.

**Answer to Question 3**

**Sodium** (2, 8, 1) loses its outer electron: $\mathrm{Na^{+}}$ (11 protons, 10 electrons).

**Chlorine** (2, 8, 7) gains it: $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$ (17 protons, 18 electrons). Both now have a full outer shell.

**Answer to Question 4**

Magnesium (2, 8, 2) must **lose 2 electrons**, but each chlorine can take **only 1**. So it forms $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and two $\mathrm{Cl^{-}}$: $\mathrm{MgCl_2}$.

items.prompt: Which figure shows the magnesium oxide formed when magnesium (2, 8, 2) reacts with oxygen (2, 6)?

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: Mg gives **both** outer electrons to O: $\mathrm{Mg^{2+}}$ and $\mathrm{O^{2-}}$. (a) moves one electron, (b) the wrong way, (d) shares them.

items.text:
**What this shows**

The same circuit with common salt as a solid, dissolved in water, and molten. Circles with + and − are the ions.

**Answer to Question 5**

A current needs **charged particles that can move**. In the solid the ions are **locked** in a rigid structure; in water or when melted, the ions **move** to the oppositely charged electrodes.

**What this shows**

Melting and boiling points of some ionic compounds, in kelvin.

items.prompt: Which of these will light a bulb in a circuit? (i) dry sodium chloride crystals, (ii) sodium chloride solution, (iii) sodium chloride stirred into kerosene, (iv) molten magnesium chloride

items.text:
**On this question**

**C**: in (ii) and (iv) the ions can **move**. In (i) they are fixed, and in (iii) the salt does not dissolve.

items.text:
**What this shows**

The steps of extraction for metals of high, medium and low reactivity, from the ore to the pure metal.

**Answer to Question 6**

Gold and silver are at the **bottom** of the series and hardly react, so they stay **free**; sodium is so **reactive** it is always combined.

items.text:
**Answer to Question 7**

**(a)** $\mathrm{Fe_{2}O_{3}}$ + $\mathrm{2Al}$ $\longrightarrow$ $\mathrm{2Fe}$ + $\mathrm{Al_{2}O_{3}}$ + heat. Aluminium is above iron, so it takes the oxygen.

**(b)** The reaction gives out so much heat that the iron is produced **molten**: the **thermit reaction**, used to join railway tracks and cracked machine parts.

items.prompt: In $\mathrm{3MnO_2 + 4Al \longrightarrow 3Mn + 2Al_2O_3}$, which substance is reduced and which is the reducing agent?
options: Al is reduced; $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ is the reducing agent
$\mathrm{MnO_2}$ is reduced; Al is the reducing agent
Mn is reduced; $\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ is the reducing agent
$\mathrm{Al_2O_3}$ is reduced; Mn is the reducing agent

items.text:
**On this question**

**B**: $\mathrm{MnO_2}$ **loses oxygen**, so it is reduced; aluminium **gains oxygen** (is oxidised), so it is the reducing agent.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Electrolytic refining of copper: an impure copper anode and a pure copper cathode in acidified copper sulphate solution.

**Answer to Question 8**

**(a)** The impure **anode thins** as its copper dissolves as $\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}$; the pure **cathode thickens** as copper deposits.

**(b)** Insoluble impurities: **anode mud**.

items.prompt: In the electrolytic refining of silver, what would you take as the anode, the cathode and the electrolyte?
options: impure silver; pure silver strip; silver nitrate solution
pure silver strip; impure silver; silver nitrate solution
impure silver; pure silver strip; copper sulphate solution
impure silver; copper strip; silver nitrate solution

items.text:
**On this question**

**A**: anode: impure silver. Cathode: a thin strip of pure silver. Electrolyte: a solution of a silver salt, such as silver nitrate.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Five ways of protecting iron: (a) a gate, (b) a bicycle chain, (c) a bucket and roofing sheet, (d) a tap, (e) plates, a tumbler and spoons.

**Answer to Question 9**

**(a)** Painting, **(b)** oiling, **(c)** galvanising, **(d)** chrome plating, **(e)** alloying (stainless steel).

Paint and oil **keep air and water out**.

script.x: Show the key idea, then the five pictures. Pointer 1 sets them up.
Question 9. Answer is on pointer 2.

items.text:
**What this shows**

Galvanised iron and painted iron, both scratched and left in the rain.

**Answer to Question 10**

**Galvanising** coats iron with **zinc**, which is **more reactive** than iron, so zinc reacts first even where the coat is broken. Paint only covers the iron.

items.prompt: Name the alloy, in order: (i) copper and zinc, (ii) lead and tin, used to join electrical wires, (iii) iron with nickel and chromium.
Why is jewellery made of 22-carat gold and not 24-carat gold?
options: 24-carat gold is very soft; alloying makes it harder
22-carat gold has a higher melting point

items.text:
**On Question 1**

**B**: brass (Cu + Zn), solder (Pb + Sn), stainless steel (Fe + Ni + Cr).

**On Question 2**

**B**: pure (24-carat) gold is very **soft**; alloying it with copper or silver makes it **harder**.
